column1: # topic: Chapter 7: The American People and the American Revolution, 1775-1783

column2: John Adams, John Dickinson, Benjamin Franklin, Thomas Jefferson, Richard Henry Lee and John Hancock were members of the Second Continental Congress.
John Dickinson wrote the Olive Branch Petition.
Richard Henry Lee introduced the June 1776 motion for independence.
Thomas Jefferson did most of the drafting of the Declaration of Independence.
John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman, Robert Livingston and Thomas Jefferson formed the committee that drafted the Declaration.
Lord Dunmore was Virginia's royal governor who offered freedom to slaves who joined the British and shelled Norfolk.
Abigail Adams asked her husband to "Remember the Ladies" and limit husbands' power in the new laws.
George Washington was the Seven Years' War veteran named commander in chief of the Continental Army.
The Howe brothers commanded the British army and navy, but their caution let Washington escape.
John Burgoyne was the British general who marched from Quebec and surrendered at Saratoga.
Horatio Gates commanded the Americans at Saratoga and lost at Camden.
Benedict Arnold fought at Saratoga and later turned traitor and joined the British.
Vergennes was France's foreign minister who sent secret aid to get revenge for 1763.
Baron von Steuben was a Prussian soldier who drilled the Continental Army in spring 1778.
Joseph Brant was the bilingual, literate Mohawk leader of the Iroquois warriors who aided the British.
Cornwallis led the British southern campaign and surrendered at Yorktown.
Nathanael Greene took the southern command after Camden, used militia, and divided his army to wear down Cornwallis.
Daniel Morgan led part of Greene's army and routed Tarleton at Cowpens.
Banastre Tarleton commanded the British force Morgan routed at Cowpens.
Marion, the "Swamp Fox," and Sumter, "the Gamecock," led rebel partisan bands in the southern backcountry.
Rochambeau led French troops and de Grasse a French fleet that trapped Cornwallis at Yorktown.
Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and John Jay negotiated the 1783 Treaty of Paris.
